title: How do you design a delayed job scheduler at scale — why NOT poll the DB every second (`SELECT ... WHERE execute_at <= NOW()`), and instead use time bucketing / a Redis sorted set (score = execute-at timestamp) to find due jobs efficiently?
shortTitle: How do you design a delayed job scheduler at scale?

s1_definition.profdef: A delayed job scheduler executes work at or after a future time — send a payment reminder in 24 hours, retry a failed settlement in 5 minutes, expire a hold at a specific timestamp. The naive design polls a relational table every second with a query like select where execute_at is less than or equal to now, but this does not scale because every poll scans or indexes over the whole table, most polls return nothing (wasted work), the constant queries load the database, and you get lock contention as workers compete to claim the same due rows. The scalable design stores jobs in a structure that makes "find everything due now" cheap, most commonly a Redis sorted set where the score is the execute-at timestamp, so retrieving due jobs is a single range query from the earliest score up to the current time in logarithmic time, and jobs you are not yet due to run cost nothing to skip. Time bucketing is a complementary technique that groups jobs into per-minute or per-second buckets so each tick only looks at the relevant bucket rather than the whole dataset.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must send thousands of scheduled reminders and process timed holds. The naive clerk walks the entire filing cabinet every single second asking "is anything due yet?" — exhausting, and almost always the answer is no. The smart design is a special rack where every task is filed in order of exactly when it is due, like a row of pigeonholes labelled by time. The clerk simply glances at the front of the rack and pulls only the tasks whose due time has passed, ignoring everything filed for later entirely. Time bucketing goes further: there is one pigeonhole per minute, so at 10:05 the clerk opens only the 10:05 pigeonhole, never touching the thousands of tasks filed for later in the day. Redis's sorted set is that time-ordered rack, where the "label" is the timestamp and pulling the due ones is a single quick reach.
s1_definition.oneliner: Do not poll the whole database every second for due jobs; store jobs ordered by their execute-at time in a Redis sorted set so finding everything due now is a single logarithmic range query, and bucket by time so each tick only inspects the relevant slice.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A delayed job scheduler executes work at or after a future time — send a payment reminder in 24 hours, retry a failed settlement in 5 minutes, expire a hold at a specific timestamp. The naive design polls a relational table every second with a query like select where execute_at is less than or equal to now, but this does not scale because every poll scans or indexes over the whole table, most polls return nothing (wasted work), the constant queries load the database, and you get lock contention as workers compete to claim the same due rows. Time bucketing is a complementary technique that groups jobs into per-minute or per-second buckets so each tick only looks at the relevant bucket rather than the whole dataset.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must send thousands of scheduled reminders and process timed holds. The naive clerk walks the entire filing cabinet every single second asking "is anything due yet?" — exhausting, and almost always the answer is no. The smart design is a special rack where every task is filed in order of exactly when it is due, like a row of pigeonholes labelled by time. The clerk simply glances at the front of the rack and pulls only the tasks whose due time has passed, ignoring everything filed for later entirely. Time bucketing goes further: there is one pigeonhole per minute, so at 10:05 the clerk opens only the 10:05 pigeonhole, never touching the thousands of tasks filed for later in the day. Redis's sorted set is that time-ordered rack, where the "label" is the timestamp and pulling the due ones is a single quick reach.

**One line to remember:** Do not poll the whole database every second for due jobs; store jobs ordered by their execute-at time in a Redis sorted set so finding everything due now is a single logarithmic range query, and bucket by time so each tick only inspects the relevant slice.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem with polling a relational table every second is a combination of waste, load, and contention. Even with an index on the execute_at column, every poll runs a query, and the vast majority of polls return nothing because most jobs are not yet due, so you are paying for a query a second (or more, across many worker instances) just to usually get an empty result. As the table grows to millions of rows, the index scans get more expensive and the constant query traffic competes with the real transactional workload for database resources. Worst of all, when jobs do become due, multiple worker instances all run the same claiming query and fight over the same rows, producing lock contention and the risk of two workers grabbing the same job. Polling can work at small scale, but it degrades badly as job volume and worker count grow.

The core of the scalable design is a data structure where "give me everything due up to now" is cheap. A Redis sorted set is the canonical choice: you add each job with the ZADD command using the execute-at timestamp (as epoch milliseconds) as the score and the job id as the member, for example `ZADD due_jobs 1735000000000 job:TXN-reminder-88`. Because a sorted set keeps members ordered by score, finding due jobs is a single range query `ZRANGEBYSCORE due_jobs -inf <now>`, which returns only the jobs whose scheduled time has passed, in time proportional to the log of the set size plus the number returned. Crucially, the millions of jobs scheduled for the future cost nothing to skip, because the structure is ordered and you only read from the due end. Scheduling a new job is a logarithmic ZADD, and rescheduling is just updating the score.

To claim jobs safely so that two workers never run the same one, you make the fetch-and-remove atomic. The clean way is a short Lua script that runs `ZRANGEBYSCORE` for due jobs and then `ZREM` to remove them in the same atomic server-side operation, so whichever worker's script runs first gets the jobs and removes them, and the others see them gone. Alternatively you move claimed jobs to an in-progress structure in the same atomic step. Because Redis executes commands and scripts serially on one thread, this atomicity is guaranteed without distributed locks, which is a major reason the sorted-set approach is both fast and correct under many competing workers.

Time bucketing is the complementary technique for very high volume. Instead of one giant sorted set, you partition jobs into buckets keyed by time granularity, for example one sorted set or list per minute named by the minute timestamp, such as `jobs:2026-10-24T17:25`. The scheduler, on each tick, only looks at the current (and any missed past) bucket, so the amount of data inspected per tick is bounded by what is actually due in that window rather than the whole dataset. Bucketing also spreads the data across keys, which matters in a sharded Redis Cluster because different buckets can live on different shards, distributing both storage and load. A refinement is to shard a hot bucket further by hashing the job id so that a single very busy minute does not concentrate on one key or one worker.

The scheduler-worker split (which the detailed follow-up question explores) is part of the design: a lightweight scheduler process repeatedly pops due jobs from the sorted set or current bucket and enqueues them onto a normal work queue, and a pool of workers consumes that queue to do the actual work. This separates deciding when a job runs from deciding how it runs, lets you scale workers independently, and keeps the time-ordered structure small because jobs leave it as soon as they are due.

Durability and recovery matter because Redis is primarily in-memory. You enable Redis persistence (append-only file) so the sorted set survives a restart, and for strong durability you keep the authoritative job definitions in a relational store and use Redis as the fast time index, reconciling periodically so a lost Redis entry can be rebuilt. You also handle the case where the scheduler is down for a while: because due jobs simply accumulate in the past range of the sorted set, when the scheduler recovers its next range query naturally picks up everything that became due during the outage, so no job is silently skipped — they just run late, which is usually acceptable for delayed jobs.

A senior nuance is choosing the right tool for the scale and guarantees you need. For modest scale, a well-indexed relational table with a sensible poll interval and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to avoid contention is perfectly fine and simpler to operate. The Redis sorted set shines at high volume and high scheduling churn. For extreme scale or stronger ordering and delivery guarantees, purpose-built systems like a message broker with delayed delivery, or a dedicated scheduler, may be warranted. The key interview point is to articulate why naive per-second polling of the whole table does not scale — wasted empty polls, database load, and claim contention — and to propose a time-ordered structure (sorted set) plus bucketing that makes finding due jobs cheap and claiming them atomic.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India needs to schedule millions of delayed jobs: payment reminders, settlement retries, and hold expirations, each with a specific future execute time.

Problem 1 — The first version polled a jobs table every second with a select-where-execute-at-before-now query, and as the table grew to millions of rows the constant empty polls loaded the database and multiple workers fought over the same due rows. This is the don't-poll-the-whole-DB problem.

Problem 2 — The team replaced it with a Redis sorted set scored by execute-at time, so finding due jobs became a single range query that skips all future jobs for free. This is the sorted-set time-index solution.

Problem 3 — At peak, a single busy minute had tens of thousands of due jobs, so the team bucketed jobs per minute and sharded hot buckets, and made the claim atomic so no two workers ran the same job. This is the time-bucketing and atomic-claim refinement.

We will model a scheduler that stores jobs in a time-ordered structure scored by execute-at, fetches due jobs with a range query, claims them atomically so no duplicate execution, buckets by minute, and contrasts the cost against naive full-table polling.

The code will have a `Job` with an execute-at time, a `SortedSetScheduler` emulating Redis ZADD and ZRANGEBYSCORE with atomic claim, a `MinuteBucketIndex` for time bucketing, and a demo that schedules jobs, advances a simulated clock, and pulls due jobs efficiently while skipping future ones.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac DelayedSchedulerDemo.java
java DelayedSchedulerDemo

# Why NOT poll the whole DB every second:
#   most polls return nothing (wasted), constant queries load the DB,
#   workers fight over the same due rows (lock contention).
# Scalable design:
#   ZADD due_jobs <execute_at_ms> <jobId>      # O(log N) schedule
#   ZRANGEBYSCORE due_jobs -inf <now>          # O(log N + M) find due; future skipped free
#   atomic Lua ZRANGEBYSCORE + ZREM            # no duplicate execution
#   bucket per minute (jobs:<minute>) + shard hot buckets by hash(jobId)
# Small scale fallback: indexed table + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four jobs scheduled at future times — two reminders due at now+1000, a settlement retry at now+2000, and a hold expiry at now+5000 — using a simulated clock.

Step 1 — Each job is scheduled with its execute-at timestamp as the sort score, the equivalent of a Redis ZADD. The structure keeps them ordered by time, so the earliest-due jobs are always at the front. Scheduling is a logarithmic insert, not a table scan.

Step 2 — The clock advances to now+1000 and the scheduler asks for due jobs. The range query returns only the two reminders whose time has arrived, and it does this by reading from the due end of the ordered structure, never looking at the settlement retry or the hold expiry scheduled for later. Those future jobs cost nothing to skip.

Step 3 — The two due reminders are claimed atomically, meaning they are read and removed in one indivisible step, so if several worker instances ticked at once only one would get them and the others would see them already gone — no duplicate execution and no lock fight.

Step 4 — The clock advances to now+2000 and another range query returns just the settlement retry, which has now become due. The hold expiry at now+5000 remains untouched in the structure. At no point did the scheduler scan the whole dataset.

Step 5 — The time-bucketing demo groups jobs into per-minute buckets, and the scheduler inspecting the current minute's bucket sees only the jobs in that minute, never touching the next minute's bucket. At high volume this bounds the work per tick to what is actually due in that window, and different buckets can live on different Redis shards.

```
2026-10-24 17:25:55 [INFO] Scheduled 4 jobs (ordered by execute_at)
2026-10-24 17:25:55 [INFO] Tick @1001000: claimed 2 due job(s): reminder:SAV2001 reminder:CUR3001
2026-10-24 17:25:55 [INFO] Remaining future jobs untouched: 2
2026-10-24 17:25:55 [INFO] Tick @1002000: claimed 1 due job(s): settle-retry:TXN88
2026-10-24 17:25:55 [INFO] Minute bucket @1,000,000 has 2 jobs; next-minute bucket NOT scanned this tick
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Schedule job (execute_at = future time)
    │ ZADD due_jobs <execute_at_ms> <jobId>     O(log N)
    ▼
  Redis Sorted Set (ordered by score = execute_at)
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ t+1000: reminder:SAV2001, reminder:CUR3001    │ ← due end
    │ t+2000: settle-retry:TXN88                    │
    │ t+5000: hold-expire:CUR3001                   │ ← future (skipped free)
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │ every tick:
    ▼
  ZRANGEBYSCORE due_jobs -inf <now>   (atomic Lua + ZREM = claim once)
    │ returns ONLY due jobs; future never scanned
    ▼
  enqueue due jobs → work queue → worker pool executes
    │
  (scheduler down a while? due jobs accumulate in past range → picked up on recovery)

  NAIVE (bad): SELECT ... WHERE execute_at<=NOW() every second
    → mostly empty, loads DB, workers fight over rows
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A delayed job scheduler runs work at or after a future time — a payment reminder in a day, a settlement retry in five minutes, a hold that expires at a specific timestamp. The naive design polls a relational table every second with a select-where-execute-at-is-before-now query, and I can explain precisely why that does not scale. Even with an index, every poll runs a query and most polls return nothing because most jobs are not yet due, so you pay constantly for usually-empty results, the query traffic loads the database as the table grows to millions of rows, and when jobs do become due, multiple workers run the same claiming query and fight over the same rows, causing lock contention and the risk of double execution.

The scalable design stores jobs in a structure where finding everything due now is cheap, and the canonical choice is a Redis sorted set with the execute-at timestamp as the score and the job id as the member. Because a sorted set stays ordered by score, I add a job with ZADD in logarithmic time and find due jobs with a single range query from negative infinity up to now, which returns only the jobs whose time has passed and reads from the due end, so the millions of future jobs cost nothing to skip. That is the fundamental win over polling: I never scan the whole dataset.

To claim jobs safely so two workers never run the same one, I make the fetch-and-remove atomic with a short Lua script that does the range query and the removal in one indivisible server-side step. Because Redis executes serially on one thread, that atomicity is guaranteed without any distributed lock, so the sorted-set approach is both fast and correct under many competing workers. For very high volume I add time bucketing, partitioning jobs into per-minute buckets so each tick only inspects the current bucket rather than the whole set, and I shard a hot bucket further by hashing the job id so a single busy minute does not concentrate on one key or one worker.

I pair this with a scheduler-worker split: a lightweight scheduler pops due jobs and enqueues them onto a normal work queue, and a pool of workers does the actual work, which lets me scale workers independently and keeps the time-ordered structure small. For durability I enable Redis persistence so the set survives a restart and keep the authoritative job definitions in a relational store, reconciling periodically. And because due jobs simply accumulate in the past range during any scheduler outage, when the scheduler recovers its next range query naturally picks them all up, so jobs run late rather than being lost.

In my banking work I used exactly this to schedule millions of reminders, settlement retries, and hold expirations, after the original per-second table polling started loading the database and causing workers to collide on due rows. The nuance I always add is to match the tool to the scale: at modest volume a well-indexed table polled with select-for-update-skip-locked is perfectly fine and simpler to operate, the Redis sorted set shines at high volume and high scheduling churn, and for extreme scale or stronger delivery guarantees a broker with delayed delivery or a dedicated scheduler may be warranted. The core interview point is that naive per-second polling wastes work, loads the database, and causes claim contention, and a time-ordered sorted set with bucketing and atomic claim fixes all three.

Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
